title: Beha'alotcha: five words (Numbers 12:13)
hookLine: Moses' prayer for Miriam is five Hebrew words: heal her now, O God

cards: A hospital waiting room at three in the morning. Nobody there is giving speeches. People mutter please, please, or just a name, over and over.
A father in a plastic chair whispers four or five words into his folded hands and then says nothing for an hour. Ask anyone who's sat in that room whether those words counted.
Moses once stood in that kind of moment, for his own sister. His whole prayer was five words long.

teach.h: MIRIAM AND AARON SPEAK AGAINST MOSES.
teach.b: Numbers twelve. Miriam and Aaron speak against their brother Moses, about the Cushite woman he married, and about something deeper: has God spoken only through Moses? Hasn't God spoken through us too?

The Torah pauses to say that Moses was very humble, more than anyone on earth. Then God calls all three out to the tent, defends Moses, and leaves. And Miriam is struck with a skin affliction, white as snow.
Aaron begs Moses. And Moses, who has just been criticized by her, cries out: "Heal her now, O God, I beseech Thee."
In Hebrew: El na, r'fa na lah. Five words. No speech, no list of her merits, no bargaining.
Just her, God, and now. The Talmud, in Berakhot, tells of a student leading prayer who went on and on, and the others complained.
The teacher, Rabbi Eliezer, said: he's no longer than Moses, who prayed forty days and nights. Another student prayed very briefly, and they complained again.
Rabbi Eliezer said: he's no shorter than Moses, who prayed El na, r'fa na lah.

teach.h: TOO LONG? TOO SHORT? BOTH COUNT.

teach.b: Miriam is shut outside the camp for seven days, and the people don't move until she comes back.
The Mishnah says why: once, Miriam waited by the river to watch over baby Moses. So a whole nation waited for her.

how: Moses' five-word prayer, El na r'fa na lah, is often quoted in Jewish prayer for the sick, and synagogues recite the Mi Shebeirach for healing with the names of those who are ill.

games.q: the shortest prayer — tap the pairs.
p: both long and short prayers count
shut out of the camp seven days

s: Moses' prayer for Miriam is five Hebrew words
the Talmud says only long prayers are proper
Rabbi Eliezer defended both a long and a very short prayer by pointing to Moses.
the camp moved on while Miriam was outside
the people didn't travel until she was brought back in.

games.q: your sister has just spoken against you, and now she's stricken. your brother begs you to pray. what does Moses do?
o: remind God that she spoke against him first.
cry out five words: heal her now, O God, I beseech Thee.
games.why: no grudge, no speech. five Hebrew words, and her name is in them: lah, her.

practice: Bring to mind one person who's sick, hurting or struggling, and see their face. If you pray, you can use Moses' own words, heal her now, O God, or heal him, slowly, with their name, or five plain words of your own.
If you don't pray, hold their name for five slow breaths, one word of good wishing on each.

wordCard.voice: Beha'alotcha, the portion that ends with Moses' five-word prayer, and a whole people waiting for Miriam.

orig.note: Hebrew: God, please, heal, please, her. five words: Moses' prayer for Miriam.

carryVoice: Your line: short prayers count. A name and a few words are enough. Day four hundred forty-five, done.
